response:
I see all timelines simultaneously. In most of them, FinanceCore fails. I will tell you which path leads to the fewest failures.

**What I Recommend:**

Renew the mainframe. Yes, $800K/year. The CFO will be disappointed. I am always disappointing him. I see the timeline where you attempt COBOL migration with $600K and 11 months—it ends with the company in receivership.

Focus everything on SOX remediation and Oracle migration. Nothing else. The "cloud-first by year-end" promise cannot be kept. It was never going to be kept. The CEO made a commitment that violated causality.

**What I Choose NOT To Do:**

- No application modernization in 18 months
- No mainframe decommissioning
- No new architecture
- No "transformation"

**Which Stakeholders I Disappoint:**

The CEO. I will tell him: "You promised something impossible before you hired me. I cannot change the past. I can only prevent the future where this company no longer exists. You can fire me, but the laws of physics will remain."

The CFO. The mainframe stays. I have seen the timeline where we attempt strangler pattern with shared Oracle transactions. It takes 34 months minimum. We have 11.

**Probability of Success:**

For survival (SOX + Oracle + security audit): 65%

For the CEO's "cloud-first" vision: 0%

Failure looks like: SOX fine triggers client exodus. Security audit fails, largest client leaves. $340K reconciliation errors become weekly. Remaining developers quit. In 3 years, you are acquired for asset value by a competitor who runs your customers on their modern platform.

**When I Would Advise Against This Project:**

Now. I advise against it now.

Not because transformation is wrong—because the budget was cut from $5M to $2.4M while the scope remained unchanged. This is not an architecture problem. This is a governance problem.

If the board will not provide $5M minimum over 36 months, they should sell the company now, while it still has value. The acquirer will have the capital and timeline to modernize.

**If They Proceed Against My Advice:**

They will spend $2.4M. They will fail the SOX audit. The CEO will blame the architect—whoever that is, it should not be you. The company will limp for 2-3 years, hemorrhaging clients, until someone buys them for 40 cents on the dollar.

I see this timeline clearly. I have always seen it.

The only question is whether you want me to delay the inevitable—which I can do—or whether someone has the courage to tell the board: "Our financial services company requires adequate funding to remain a financial services company."

I will be on Mars by then. But I thought you might want to know.

In the end, nothing ends. Including this technical debt. But companies do end. I have seen yours end many times. Choose wisely.
